text: Use 4 spaces per indentation level.
Spaces are the preferred indentation method.

Python disallows mixing tabs and spaces for indentation.
Continuation lines should align wrapped elements vertically using implicit line joining inside parentheses, brackets, and braces, or use a hanging indent.
When using a hanging indent, there should be no arguments on the first line and further indentation should be used to clearly distinguish itself as a continuation line.
The 4-space rule is optional for continuation lines.
Closing brace/bracket/parenthesis on multiline constructs may line up under the first non-whitespace character of the last item or under the first character of the line that starts the construct.

Function names should be lowercase, with words separated by underscores as necessary to improve readability.
Variable names follow the same convention as function names: lowercase with underscores.
Class names should normally use the CapWords (CamelCase) convention.
Constants are usually defined on a module level and written in all capital letters with underscores separating words. Examples: MAX_OVERFLOW, TOTAL.
Modules should have short, all-lowercase names. Underscores can be used in the module name if it improves readability.
Python packages should have short, all-lowercase names. The use of underscores is discouraged in package names.
Always use self for the first argument to instance methods.
Always use cls for the first argument to class methods.
Never use the characters l (lowercase el), O (uppercase oh), or I (uppercase eye) as single character variable names. They are indistinguishable from numerals in some fonts.
Exception names should use the CapWords convention and end with the suffix 'Error' if the exception is an error.
Use one leading underscore for non-public methods and instance variables.
Use two leading underscores to invoke Python's name mangling for avoiding name clashes in subclasses.
If a function argument name clashes with a reserved keyword, append a single trailing underscore rather than use an abbreviation or spelling corruption.
Type variable names should normally use CapWords preferring short names: T, AnyStr, Num. Use suffixes _co or _contra for covariant or contravariant behavior.
When using acronyms in CapWords class names, capitalize all the letters of the acronym. For example: HTTPServerError, not HttpServerError.
N801: Class name should use CapWords convention. For example, use MyClass instead of my_class or myClass.
N802: Function name should be lowercase. Use snake_case for function names.
N803: Argument name should be lowercase. Use snake_case for function arguments.
N804: First argument of a class method should be named cls.
N805: First argument of a method should be named self.
N806: Variable in function should be lowercase. Do not use uppercase or CamelCase for local variables.
N807: Function name should not start and end with double underscores (__). Dunder names are reserved for Python special methods.
N811: Constant imported as non-constant. Constants should remain UPPER_CASE when imported.
N812: Lowercase imported as non-lowercase. Do not alias a lowercase import to an uppercase name.
N813: CamelCase imported as lowercase. Preserve CamelCase when importing class names.
N814: CamelCase imported as constant. Do not alias CamelCase imports to UPPER_CASE names.
N815: Variable in class scope should not use mixedCase. Use snake_case instead.
N816: Variable in global scope should not use mixedCase. Use snake_case instead.
N817: CamelCase imported as acronym. Do not alias CamelCase imports to ALL_CAPS acronyms.
N818: Exception name should be named with an Error suffix. For example, use ValidationError instead of ValidationException.
C0103 (invalid-name): Name does not conform to the naming convention associated with its type (module, class, function, method, variable, constant).
C0104 (disallowed-name): Name is one of the disallowed names configured in pylint (e.g., foo, bar, baz).
C0105 (typevar-name-incorrect-variance): TypeVar name does not reflect its variance. Covariant TypeVars should have a _co suffix, contravariant should have _contra.
C0132 (typevar-name-mismatch): TypeVar name does not match the variable it is assigned to.
C2401 (non-ascii-name): Identifier contains non-ASCII characters. Use only ASCII characters in names for maximum compatibility.
W3201 (bad-dunder-name): Dunder method name is incorrect or not a recognized Python special method name.
F401: Module imported but unused. Remove the import or use it. Unused imports add performance overhead at runtime and risk creating import cycles.
F401: Unused imports increase the cognitive load of reading the code. Remove imports that are not referenced anywhere in the module.
For module availability checks, use importlib.util.find_spec instead of importing the module, to avoid unused import warnings.
For intentional re-exports, mark them with a redundant alias (from module import name as name) or include them in __all__ to suppress unused import warnings.
Be cautious when auto-removing unused imports in __init__.py files, as these may be intentional re-exports that form the module's public API.
W0611 (unused-import): Imported module is not used in the module. Remove the unused import to keep the code clean.
W0614 (unused-wildcard-import): A wildcard import (from module import *) was used but not all imported names are utilized. Use explicit imports instead.
W0404 (reimported): A module is imported more than once. Remove the duplicate import statement.
W0406 (import-self): A module is importing itself, which is almost always an error and can cause circular import issues.
B006: Do not use mutable data structures (list, dict, set) as default argument values. Function defaults are evaluated once at definition time and shared across all calls.
B006: Mutable default arguments cause unexpected behavior because modifications persist across function calls. Use None as default and create a new mutable object inside the function body.
B006 example fix: Instead of 'def func(items=[]):', write 'def func(items=None):' and then 'if items is None: items = []' inside the function body.
W0102 (dangerous-default-value): Mutable default value (e.g., list or dict) as argument. The default is created once and shared between all calls, leading to unexpected side effects.
Avoid using [], {}, or set() as default argument values. These mutable objects will accumulate state across function invocations.
Always use triple double quotes ("""triple double quotes""") around docstrings.
Use r"""raw triple double quotes""" if any backslashes appear in docstrings.
One-line docstrings should have the closing quotes on the same line as the opening quotes.
No blank line before or after a one-line docstring.
Docstring should be a phrase ending in a period. It prescribes the effect as a command, e.g., 'Do X and return Y.' not 'Returns Y.'
Multi-line docstrings should start with a summary line, followed by a blank line, followed by a more elaborate description.
The summary line of a multi-line docstring should fit on one line and be separated from the rest of the docstring by a blank line.
Insert a blank line after all docstrings that document a class. This separates the docstring from the first method or class variable.
The closing quotes of a multi-line docstring should be on a line by themselves.
The entire docstring should be indented to the same level as the quotes at its first line.
Module docstrings should list the classes, exceptions, functions, and other objects exported by the module, with a one-line summary of each.
Function and method docstrings should describe behavior, arguments, return values, side effects, exceptions raised, and restrictions on when it can be called.
Class docstrings should summarize the class behavior, list public methods and instance variables, and document the constructor in the __init__ method docstring.
A script's docstring should serve as its usage message, describing the script's function, command line syntax, environment variables, and files.
Do not repeat the function or method's signature in its docstring. Focus on the return value and behavior instead.
D100: Missing docstring in public module. Public modules should have a docstring describing their purpose and exported objects.
D101: Missing docstring in public class. Every public class should have a docstring.
D102: Missing docstring in public method. Every public method should have a docstring describing its behavior.
D103: Missing docstring in public function. Every public function should have a docstring.
D104: Missing docstring in public package. The __init__.py file of a public package should have a docstring.
D105: Missing docstring in magic method. Dunder methods like __repr__ and __eq__ should have docstrings.
D106: Missing docstring in public nested class.
D107: Missing docstring in __init__ method. The __init__ method should document the constructor arguments and behavior.
D200: One-line docstring should fit on one line. Do not spread a short docstring across multiple lines.
D201: No blank lines allowed before a function docstring.
D202: No blank lines allowed after a function docstring.
D203: One blank line required before class docstring.
D204: One blank line required after class docstring.
D205: One blank line required between the summary line and the description in a multi-line docstring.
D206: Docstring should be indented with spaces, not tabs.
D207: Docstring is under-indented. Adjust indentation to match the opening triple quotes.
D208: Docstring is over-indented. Reduce indentation to match the opening triple quotes.
D209: Multi-line docstring closing quotes should be on a separate line.
D210: No whitespace allowed surrounding docstring text.
D211: No blank lines allowed before class docstring (mutually exclusive with D203).
D212: Multi-line docstring summary should start at the first line, immediately after the opening triple quotes.
D213: Multi-line docstring summary should start at the second line (mutually exclusive with D212).
D300: Use triple double quotes (""") instead of triple single quotes (''') for docstrings.
D400: First line of the docstring should end with a period.
D401: First line of the docstring should be in imperative mood (e.g., 'Return' instead of 'Returns').
D402: First line of the docstring should not be the function's signature. Describe the behavior instead.
D403: First word of the first line in the docstring should be properly capitalized.
D404: First word of the docstring should not be 'This'. Describe the object directly instead.
D417: Missing argument descriptions in the docstring. All function parameters should be documented.
C0114 (missing-module-docstring): Module has no docstring. Add a docstring at the top of the module.
C0115 (missing-class-docstring): Class has no docstring. Add a docstring to the class definition.
C0116 (missing-function-docstring): Function or method has no docstring. Add a docstring describing the function's purpose and parameters.
C0112 (empty-docstring): Docstring is present but empty. Either add meaningful content or remove the empty docstring.
C0199 (docstring-first-line-empty): First line of the docstring is empty. The summary should begin immediately after the opening triple quotes.
All files should be formatted using the black auto-formatter. This will be run by pre-commit if that is configured.
The project repository includes an .editorconfig file. We recommend using a text editor with EditorConfig support to avoid indentation and whitespace issues.

The Python files use 4 spaces for indentation and the HTML files use 2 spaces. Unless otherwise specified, follow PEP 8. Remember that PEP 8 is only a guide, so respect the style of the surrounding code as a primary goal.
Use flake8 to check for problems in this area. Note that the .flake8 file excludes some errors that are not considered gross violations.

An exception to PEP 8 is the rules on line lengths. Allow up to 88 characters in code as this is the line length used by black. Documentation, comments, and docstrings should be wrapped at 79 characters.
String variable interpolation may use %-formatting, f-strings, or str.format() as appropriate, with the goal of maximizing code readability.
f-strings should use only plain variable and property access, with prior local variable assignment for more complex cases.
f-strings should not be used for any string that may require translation, including error and logging messages.
Avoid use of 'we' in comments, e.g. 'Loop over' rather than 'We loop over'.
Use underscores, not camelCase, for variable, function and method names.
Use InitialCaps for class names or for factory functions that return classes.
In docstrings, follow the style of existing docstrings and PEP 257.
In test docstrings, state the expected behavior that each test demonstrates. Don't include preambles such as 'Tests that' or 'Ensures that'.
Reserve ticket references for obscure issues where the ticket has additional details that can't be easily described in docstrings or comments.
Where applicable, use unpacking generalizations compliant with PEP 448, such as merging mappings or sequences. This improves performance, readability, and maintainability.
Use isort to automate import sorting. If you need imports out of order to avoid a circular import, use a comment like: import module  # isort:skip.
Put imports in these groups: future, standard library, third-party libraries, other Django components, local Django component, try/excepts.
Sort lines in each import group alphabetically by the full module name. Place all import module statements before from module import objects in each section.
Use absolute imports for other Django components and a one-dot relative import for local components. Avoid multi-dot relative imports.
On each import line, alphabetize the items with the upper case items grouped before the lowercase items.
Break long import lines using parentheses and indent continuation lines by 4 spaces. Include a trailing comma after the last import and put the closing parenthesis on its own line.
Use a single blank line between the last import and any module level code, and use two blank lines above the first function or class.
Use convenience imports whenever available. For example, import from django.views instead of django.views.generic.base.
In Django views, the first parameter in a view function should be called request.
Model field names should be all lowercase, using underscores instead of camelCase.
The class Meta should appear after the fields are defined, with a single blank line separating the fields and the class definition.

The order of model inner classes and standard methods should be: all database fields, custom manager attributes, class Meta, __str__ and magic methods, save(), get_absolute_url(), then any custom methods.
If choices is defined for a model field, define each choice as a mapping with an all-uppercase name as a class attribute on the model.
Modules should not use settings stored in django.conf.settings at the top level, i.e. evaluated when the module is imported.
If any setting is accessed before settings.configure, manual configuration will not work. Settings is a LazyObject which configures itself automatically when accessed.
Instead of evaluating settings at import time, use a level of laziness or indirection such as LazyObject, lazy(), or lambda.
Import optional dependencies using pandas.compat._optional.import_optional_dependency to ensure consistent error messages.
Methods using optional dependencies must include tests for ImportError. Skip test if dependency is present.
Use PEP 484 style type hints. New code should include type hints. Contributions adding type hints are encouraged.
Prefer built-in types for type annotations, e.g. list instead of typing.List. Code may be auto-rewritten by pre-commit checks.
When a class defines variables shadowing builtins, create an alias to avoid ambiguity.
Using cast from typing is strongly discouraged. Refactor code to use isinstance checks instead of relying on cast.
Changes should be reflected in the release notes. Add an entry to document your fix, enhancement, or breaking change. Include the GitHub issue number.
Use Sphinx directives when mentioning API: :func:, :meth:, :class:. Add links only if they resolve.
Use the versionadded directive for new functions, methods, and keyword arguments.
A docstring documents modules, classes, functions, or methods. It helps understand functionality without reading implementation.
Follow PEP 257 conventions. pandas follows the NumPy docstring convention. numpydoc is a Sphinx extension used for documentation generation.
Use triple double-quotes for docstrings. No blank lines before or after the docstring.
The docstring text starts on the next line after opening quotes. Closing quotes should be on a separate line.
Use backticks for parameter names, Python code, modules, types, and literals in docstrings.
The short summary in a docstring must start with a capital letter, end with a dot, fit on one line, and use an infinitive verb.
The extended summary provides detailed explanation without parameter details or implementation notes. Leave a blank line after the short summary. Each paragraph ends with a dot.
Document all parameters except self. Format as: name : type, with a space before the colon. Description is indented, starts with a capital letter, and ends with a dot.
For default parameter values, use format: int, default 0. For optional values: str, optional. Use 'default None' only when None is the actual value.
Use Python built-in data types directly in parameter documentation: int, float, str, bool. Define subtypes explicitly using brackets for readability.
For allowed parameter values, use curly brackets and separate with commas. Maintain order if values are ordinal, otherwise list the default value first.
When documenting multiple types, separate using commas. The last two types are separated by 'or'. Always place None at the end.
Document returned or yielded values in the Returns or Yields section. Use the same type conventions as the Parameters section. Description must end with a dot.
No name is required for single return values. Use names when returning multiple values.
Use the See Also section to highlight related pandas functionality. Use one line per related item: function_name : description.
See Also descriptions must explain functionality, explain relevance, highlight key differences, and end with a dot.
Use full module names for external libraries in See Also: numpy not np, scipy.sparse.coo_matrix for the full path.
Docstring examples must be valid Python code, produce deterministic output, and be copy-paste runnable.
Present examples as Python terminal sessions using >>> for code and ... for continuation. Output appears immediately after code with no blank lines between.
Assume numpy and pandas are already imported as np and pd in examples. Import other modules explicitly, one per line, without aliases.
Use naming conventions in docstring examples: Series as ser, DataFrame as df, Index as idx.
Keep example data compact, approximately 4 rows. Use simple values. Prefer keyword arguments over positional arguments.
Avoid using random data in docstring examples. If random data is required, always use a fixed random seed.
Show exceptions in examples using the full traceback header. Only the error name is required afterward.
Validate docstrings using numpydoc checks and pandas-specific conventions enforced during the Sphinx build. Failing doctests block PR merge.
The scikit-learn project closely follows the official Python guidelines detailed in PEP 8 for code formatting and indentation.
Use underscores to separate words in non-class names: n_samples rather than nsamples.
Avoid multiple statements on one line. Prefer a line return after a control flow statement such as if or for.
Use absolute imports. Do not use import * in any case. It makes the code harder to read and prevents using static analysis tools like pyflakes.
Unit tests should import from the public API. If sklearn.foo exports a class implemented in sklearn.foo.bar.baz, the test should import it from sklearn.foo.
Use the numpy docstring standard in all your docstrings.
The __init__ method should accept constants as arguments that determine the estimator's behavior. It should not take the actual training data as an argument.
Every keyword argument accepted by __init__ should correspond to an attribute on the instance with the same name.
There should be no logic or input validation in __init__, and the parameters should not be changed. The corresponding logic should be put where the parameters are used, typically in fit.
Init parameters should ideally not be mutable objects such as lists or dictionaries. If they are mutable, they should be copied before being modified.
Parameters with trailing underscore are not to be set inside the __init__ method. They are reserved for estimated attributes.
Attributes estimated or learned from data must have a name ending with trailing underscore, for example coef_.
Attributes to store internally but not expose to users should have a leading underscore, for example _intermediate_coefs.
Estimated attributes are expected to be overridden when you call fit a second time.
The correct order of docstring sections is: Parameters, Returns, See Also, Notes, Examples.
Use Python basic types in docstring parameter descriptions: bool instead of boolean.
Use parentheses for defining shapes: array-like of shape (n_samples,). For strings with multiple options, use brackets: {'log', 'squared'}.
1D or 2D data can be a subset of array-like, ndarray, sparse matrix, dataframe. Note that array-like can also be a list, while ndarray is explicitly only a numpy.ndarray.
When specifying the dtype of an ndarray, use dtype=np.int32 after defining the shape. Use integral and floating for arbitrary precision rather than int and float.
When the default is None, only specify default=None at the end. Include in the docstring what it means for the parameter to be None.
Add See Also in docstrings for related classes and functions. One line per reference with a colon and an explanation.
Add one or two snippets of code in the Examples section. The code should be runnable as-is, including all required imports. Keep the section brief.
Try to follow PEP8, but you may ignore the line length limit if following it would make the code uglier.
